events.title: Bowen says 'no carve-outs' after Queensland claims data centre win
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy Minister says 'no carve-outs' after Queensland claims data centre win Chris Bowen has slapped down Queensland and the Northern Territory, insisting they have not been given a carve-out from new data centre rules. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Energy Minister Chris Bowen has rejected claims Queensland and the Northern Territory secured a carve-out from new rules requiring data centres to use 100 per cent renewables. States will be able to seek approval to use alternatives like coal or gas, but Mr Bowen says the Commonwealth will have the final say and the threshold will be "very high". The federal government will release draft national data centre standards before seeking to pass the legislation early next year. Queensland and the Northern Territory will not have control over how data centres are powered, the federal government insists, declaring there will be "no exceptions and no carve-outs" under its renewables plan. Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen told the ABC the national standards governing the development of data centres in Australia would still require them to bring their own "100 per cent" renewable energy plus firming through battery storage or gas. Mr Bowen has rejected claims this element of the Commonwealth's plan was watered down after a meeting of national cabinet on Wednesday where Queensland Premier David Crisafulli claimed a "win" that would allow his state to decide how data centres were powered. "So, as we said we would, we are legislating nationally consistent standards across the board with no exceptions and no carve-outs," Mr Bowen said. How Australia wants to be more than a data centre host Australia’s appeal as a destination for data centres has given it bargaining power in the AI boom. "The only change is that where a state owned government electricity company asserts that they can do it cheaper than renewables, they can apply to the Commonwealth to do that." In response, the Queensland government has now argued Mr Bowen's "rhetoric" was not contributing to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's "goal" of proving a "positive path forward" on data centres. Premiers and chief ministers signed off on new data centre standards requiring data centre operators to invest in new renewable energy to offset their power usage, but also gave flexibility for state-owned electricity assets. This was widely interpreted as a capitulation to Queensland and the Northern Territory, which had both insisted they would not be dictated to by Canberra. Mr Bowen said it would be up to the Commonwealth to "decide" whether to let states use coal or gas as a main power source, and they would have to prove it was "cheaper and better for the grid than renewables would be". "[That] is a very high bar and very difficult to do, but some states may choose to do that," he said. Mr Bowen said the Australian Energy Regulator (AER), on behalf of the Commonwealth, would consider states' applications and "make a decision". "But we will be legislating those standards, which will apply equally in Queensland and the Northern Territory as everywhere else," he said. "I think it would be very, very difficult indeed for a state energy company to establish to the Commonwealth's satisfaction that a coal arrangement will be cheaper than renewables." David Crisafulli had claimed a "win" that would allow his state to decide how data centres were powered. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) In a statement on Friday, Queensland Treasurer and Energy Minister David Janetzki said the purpose of the national data centre standards was to provide a "positive path forward and certainty for Australians, government and industry". "Chris Bowen's rhetoric is not contributing to that goal," he said. "The Queensland government will remain focused on the decisions made by national cabinet — acknowledging Queensland's unique position in owning generation and distribution assets and the energy mix that comes with that." Mr Janetzki said his government was "grateful for the maturity and pragmatism" shown by Mr Albanese. Following Wednesday's national cabinet meeting, Mr Crisafulli had told the ABC his state had been given a carve-out from the renewables policy. "It's a big win, not just for our economy, it's a big win for people's power bills as well," he said. "Because we own our assets, our distribution and our generation, we are able to control a different mixture of energy right across the board. "That new energy opportunity can be the abundance of gas we have, the surplus coal-fired power generation we have in the system, it can be renewable energy opportunities.

events.title: Embattled travel giant repaying tens of millions to overcharged clients
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Corporate Travel Management under pressure again after failing to pass on tens of millions of dollars in margins to clients Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Corporate Travel Management is refunding clients after failing to pass on travel supplier margins and rebates. ( Supplied: Corporate Travel Management ) Corporate Travel Management is in the process of refunding customers after pocketing tens of millions of dollars in margins and rebates that should have been passed onto clients. It's the latest headache for Corporate Travel, after the ABC earlier this month revealed a massive overcharging scandal relating to refugee accommodation in the UK. New chief executive Ana Pedersen says almost 80 per cent of the refunds have been agreed to or are near finalisation. An Australian travel giant arranging trips for governments and big business is in hot water after pocketing tens of millions of dollars in margins on air tickets and rebates from suppliers. Corporate Travel Management is now refunding the amounts to customers because contracts obliged the company to hand on some of this money to clients. For other customers, the problem is that contracts did not spell out what to do with the margins and so the cash is being handed back. The method of overcharging was revealed in an announcement from Brisbane-based Corporate Travel to the share market and brings the total of remediation to almost $246 million. Corporate Travel Management provides travel services to big businesses and governments. ( Supplied ) It is the latest installation of an imbroglio involving the sector repaying clients, with the ABC earlier revealing a secret government audit that warned of methods of overbilling. This latest overcharging at Corporate Travel is also separate to a massive overcharging scandal that had engulfed the company's dealings with the UK government for a refugee accommodation program. As the ABC revealed earlier this month, Corporate Travel's problems in the refugee contract included it invoicing the UK government more rooms than a hotel actually had, double-billing on some hotels, or charging for exclusive use of hotels when no exclusivity existed. Corporate Travel's new chief executive, Ana Pedersen, said almost 80 per cent of refunds had been agreed to or were near finalisation. "We recognise this has been a challenging period for investors, clients, partners and our people, and we are grateful for their ongoing support and confidence," she said. The company operated globally and clients have ranged from councils to big business, even the Australian and Queensland governments. The Queensland government said it was not one of the customers awaiting a refund. The Australian government said a review had not turned up evidence of systemic overcharging or retention of customer funds and the $13 million "relates to rebates payable to the New Zealand government". The New Zealand government declined to comment on specifics but said Corporate Travel had been cooperating about potential non-payment issues. New Corporate Travel Management CEO Ana Pedersen says it is a "challenging time" for the company and its clients. ( Supplied ) The latest overbilling included almost $29 million charged on European air fares, where Corporate Travel was buying some airline tickets and then selling them to clients with an additional margin. The company's accounts list "contractual ambiguity" here — management believed how customers were billed matched long-standing practices but now noted there was "uncertainty" about the company's contractual entitlement to keeping such margins. Another $13 million is from Australia and New Zealand, and associated with Corporate Travel keeping rebates from suppliers. Suppliers to travel management companies can be hotels, airlines or rental car firms, and they can provide commissions for bulk bookings. Corporate Travel has pocketed rebates from suppliers including hotels, airlines and rental car firms. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica ) The problem for Corporate Travel is some contracts required it to pass on rebates, and this was not done. Corporate Travel's accounts insisted that errors here were not from incorrectly billing customers. events.title: Regional powers seek off-ramp from Iran war, and other Middle East developments
events.summary: Qatar and other regional powers are seeking an off-ramp from the U.S. war Qatar and other regional powers sought an off-ramp from the war with Iran on Thursday as another tanker attack was reported in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Iranian government dismissed the Trump administration's latest sanctions. Elsewhere in the Middle East, Israel continued its attacks on Gaza and Lebanon even as the country's strikes on Gaza drew a sharp rebuke from the top diplomat overseeing the U.S.-brokered ceasefire in the territory. Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here . Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani was in Tehran on Thursday as part of Qatar's efforts to resolve the conflict between the United States and Iran. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said in a post on X that Al Thani's meeting with Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi included talks on “the efforts being made to reduce escalation,” as well as a proposed plan between Iran and Oman to allow ships safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and clear the vital commercial waterway of dangerous mines. Al Thani’s office said the prime minister emphasized the “necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighboring countries and the freedom of navigation” through the strait. He also met Thursday with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and its parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf. Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, underscored the longstanding ties between the two nations, noting that Iran supported Qatar during difficult times. Al Thani said Qatar has never hesitated to cooperate with Iran. U.S. President Donald Trump told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that he has “no time schedule” to wrap up the conflict that will reach the six-month mark on Friday. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said Thursday that it had received a report of an oil tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz. The monitoring agency, run by the British military, said that local authorities reported that the vessel was hit by an unknown projectile on Tuesday in the waters between Oman and Iran, causing it to catch fire. The crew was reported to be safe and there have been no reports of environmental damage, the UKMTO said. Oil continues to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, albeit well below prewar levels, shipping analysts say. Ship traffic through the vital waterway increased last week compared with the prior week, with the number of oil and gas carriers up 50%, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence. The U.S. government has claimed that up to 9 million barrels a day are flowing through the strait “over short time periods,” but commodities analysts at ING bank cautioned that the figure “seems aggressive.” Other ship-tracking estimates suggest it’s closer to 2 to 6 million barrels per day, ING said. Before the war, some 15 million barrels per day passed through the strait. Navy Admiral Bradley Cooper, the top U.S. military commander for the Middle East, said Thursday night that international shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz have been cleared of mines. “Today, international shipping lanes are open and momentum is building,” he said in a video posted on social media. Gulf states have not commented on the statement by U.S. Central Command, and it was not possible to independently verify the claim. Even without mines, however, ships still face threats from drones, missiles and boats as they pass through the narrow waterway. Esmail Baghaei, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, wrote late Wednesday in a social media post that the U.S. had made a coalition with Bahrain, calling it a country with “virtually no meaningful economic exchange with Iran.” In another social media post on Wednesday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf thanked China for rejecting the U.S. “economic D-Day” policies against Iran. Days after the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces announced its dissolution, Syria’s interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa appointed the former SDF leader to a position as one of his advisers. events.title: Advent, Stripe abandon $63.5b pursuit of fintech pioneer PayPal
events.summary: PayPal has struggled with modernising its payment technologies as rivals have seized market share. A consortium of Advent and Stripe has abandoned its pursuit of acquiring PayPal, ending a potential $63.5 billion deal. PayPal, an early digital payments pioneer, has struggled to modernise as competitors like Apple and Alphabet gained market share. PayPal's new CEO Enrique Lores aims to set clear financial goals and revenue targets to improve investor confidence amid past leadership changes. A consortium of buyout firm Advent and payment processor Stripe has decided to abandon its pursuit of fintech pioneer PayPal Holdings , a potential deal that would have ranked as one of the biggest ever leveraged buyouts, according to people familiar with the matter. The group is no longer pursuing a deal for PayPal , the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. It had previously offered more than US$50 billion (S$63.5 billion) for the company, people with knowledge of the matter have said. Founded in the late 1990s, PayPal was an early mover in digital payments. It has since struggled with modernising its payment technologies as rivals such as Apple and Alphabet have seized market share. Bloomberg News first revealed in February that Stripe was considering an acquisition of parts or all of PayPal, after a stock slump wiped out a chunk of its value. The takeover interest, coupled with second-quarter earnings that topped analyst estimates, has helped it recover. PayPal shares have jumped more than 40 per cent this quarter, giving the company a market value of about US$52.6 billion. San Jose, California-based PayPal ousted former chief executive Alex Chriss earlier in 2026 and replaced him with Enrique Lores, who took over the role in March. Lores said he will set specific financial goals for PayPal, change how the payments company reports earnings and assign each line of business a specific revenue target to give investors a better sense of their potential. The Wall Street Journal reported in August that PayPal had found Advent and Stripe’s initial bid insufficient and the two sides were negotiating a potential higher price. Advent and Stripe could always opt to come back at a later date if the situation changes. Representatives for Advent, PayPal and Stripe declined to comment. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Judge blocks Pentagon's Anthropic blacklist
events.summary: A federal judge on Thursday struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk , ruling that the government's actions violated Anthropic's constitutional rights. Why it matters: The ruling marks a major legal victory for Anthropic in its months-long fight with the Trump administration over how the military can use its AI models. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Rita Lin ruled that the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk was unlawful. "The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics," Lin wrote in her 59-page decision. "Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice, the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless." Lin noted that the Pentagon continued pursuing work with Anthropic even after the designation: "None of that is consistent with a genuine fear that Anthropic is a saboteur who would poison its software to harm national security." What they're saying: "We welcome the court's ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful," an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement. "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology." Catch up quick: The dispute kicked off earlier this year after Anthropic and the Pentagon clashed over the military's use of the company's AI models. The Defense Department sought to use Claude for "all lawful purposes," even in the most sensitive military and intelligence applications. Anthropic insisted that two areas remain off-limits: mass surveillance of Americans and fully autonomous weapons. The standoff escalated, with the Pentagon designating Anthropic a national security and supply-chain risk, leading the AI company to sue. What's next: The government is expected to appeal the ruling. Anthropic is also fighting a separate Pentagon designation under a different statute in the D.C. Circuit.

events.title: AI, athletes, and Keith Rabois: StrictlyVC is back in New York on September 10
events.summary: Mark your calendars: On Thursday, September 10, StrictlyVC — TechCrunch’s boutique evening series — is heading to New York’s West Village (the real one — brownstones, cobblestones, and all — not the Mission Bay stretch of San Francisco that’s earned the nickname “ Vest Village ” for all the Patagonia-clad VCs roaming around). Buy your ticket today , while there’s still availability! It’s our first New York event in two years, and after a run of great nights this year in San Francisco, L.A., and Athens, we couldn’t be more excited to be back — with a stacked lineup to match. What’s in store: We’re kicking off the night with the inimitable Keith Rabois, who recently relocated East from Silicon Valley and, true to form, seems intent on shaking things up wherever he lands. Rabois has never been shy about what he thinks is working in venture and what isn’t — he’s backed Ramp four times and invested as often in State Affairs, a company using AI and local journalists to track statehouse-level news and policy data across all 50 states. He’ll share his strong opinions on founders who raise more capital than they actually need, just because they can. And we’ll get him talking about Khosla Ventures’ boldest AI bet yet: its early $50 million check into OpenAI back in 2019 when the outfit had no clear business model — plus what he makes of the narrative that OpenAI is facing more headwinds right now than its rivals. After our sit-down with Keith, stick around for a conversation you won’t find anywhere else. Craig Shapiro’s venture firm, Collaborative Fund, is generously co-hosting the evening with us, and we’ll sit down with Shapiro and Jason Levien, CEO of D.C. United, to talk sports organizations as business investments — and the increasingly tangled intersection of sports, fandom, commerce, and community. Staying on the theme of community, we’ll dig into a conversation with two founders building for a world where AI does more — but also takes something away. Tristan Walker, who sold his last company, Walker & Company Brands (maker of Bevel), to Procter & Gamble in 2018, is back with Heirloom Craft, a startup focused on reshoring American fine craftsmanship — training a new generation of artisans and rebuilding the supply chains behind them. Walker will be joined by Brynn Putnam, who sold her last company, connected-fitness startup Mirror, to Lululemon for $500 million, just three years after it was launched. Putnam’s newest venture is Board, a game company blending physical play with AI-powered creation tools — built as something of an antidote to the isolation tech has fueled, bringing people back together around, literally, a board. Last but not least, we’re thrilled to catch up with Deven Parekh, who has co-run Insight Partners — the New York powerhouse investment firm — for more than 25 years. Insight doesn’t do a lot of press, but Parekh has agreed to pull back the curtain on how the firm is thinking about a landscape where it’s gotten harder to tell asset classes apart, as some of the biggest funds have grown exponentially larger. What we want to know: How does Insight compete in a world where capital itself is a commodity, but the potential returns on massive investments have also never been bigger? Expect a fun night all around, with drinks, hors d’oeuvres, and plenty of networking before and after the fireside chats, including with Connie Loizos, Rebecca Bellan, and other TechCrunch writers (as well as our friends from other outlets). Giant thanks again to the team at Collaborative Fund for making the night possible. More details and ticketing info right here . See you in the (real) West Village. events.title: Chinese battery giant CATL spreads investments in search of new growth drivers
events.summary: World’s largest producer of lithium-ion batteries for EVs and energy storage systems has committed over 17 billion yuan to non-battery deals Since June last year, at least seven CATL-led equity deals involving a total of over 17 billion yuan (US$2.5 billion) have been announced in non-battery industries. The sectors involved span humanoid robots, state-owned hydropower stations, artificial intelligence data centres (AIDCs) and large-language-model developer DeepSeek. The equity investments by Fujian-based CATL seemed primarily strategic, similar to its earlier playbook of forming joint ventures with carmakers and investing in EV start-ups, said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. “As the incumbent leader, sustaining market share and margins requires identifying new high-growth frontiers early and capturing first-mover advantages,” she said. “AIDC’s high-growth, high-barrier characteristics position it as a potential ‘third growth curve’ alongside EVs and energy storage systems.” CATL is the world’s largest producer of lithium-ion batteries for EVs and energy storage systems. But it is facing weakening demand for electric cars in China – the world’s largest automotive market – and intensifying competition with domestic rivals for energy storage orders in overseas markets. In May, Nasdaq-listed VNET Group, a Chinese third-party provider of neutral data centres, said two CATL-affiliates would acquire up to 38.1 per cent of its shares for US$942 million, becoming its largest shareholder. This month, Shenzhen-listed Hangzhou Zhonhen Electric, which supplies power supply systems for data centres and vehicle charging, said that it planned to sell a 49 per cent stake in the business to CATL for 4.09 billion yuan.

events.title: Major private credit fund suspends investor redemptions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Private credit firm CVS Lane joins list of firms limiting investor pullouts Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Private credit firm CVS Lane says it had significant loans to collapsed property developer Bathla. ( Supplied: Bathla website ) Stress in Australia's private credit sector is intensifying. A private lender with significant loans to collapsed developer Bathla called CVS Lane is the latest private credit firm to limit "investor redemptions". The ABC has confirmed that the investment manager told investors on Thursday that its CVS Lane First Mortgage Fund and CVS Lane Property Finance Fund had exposure to Bathla across nine different loans. Investor redemptions are when investors in private credit firms seek to get some or all of their money returned in the face of concerns about the safety of their investment because of potentially overly risky lending. Major Sydney residential developer Bathla Group announced earlier this week that it was going into administration after months of mounting financial pressure, owning more than $3.5 billion. Major NSW developer enters administration Bathla Group says tax changes, softening sales and construction costs have led to its plight. Administrators from Teneo were appointed to its main corporate entity, Universal Property Group, as well as Raj & Jai Construction, a company linked to the Bathla Group, documents lodged with ASIC show. CVS Lane is reported to have told investors it had "determined to temporarily suspend the processing of application and redemption requests across the funds". "The funds' redemption provisions are designed to balance investor liquidity with the interests of all investors in the funds," it told clients. Temporary suspension 'in best interests' CVS Lane has $2.1 billion under management. "The trustee considers a temporary suspension to be in the best interests of investors as a whole, with relevant factors including the current uncertainty surrounding the Bathla administration and the need to ensure any decisions … are made on the basis of the best available information," CVS Lane is reported to have told investors. There are about 40 private credit funds invested in Bathla, with exposures ranging from $1.5 million to $340 million. CVS Lane told investors it would update them next week and reassess its position by the end of October. Among the other private credit firms exposed to Bathla, the ABC has contacted Balmain, Centuria Bass, Credit Connect, CVS Lane, Keyview, La Trobe, Ray White Capital and Trilogy for comment. The ABC understands private credit firm Keyview's loans are at the stage of being repaid through the settlement of completed assets rather than having any exposure to Bathla's ongoing viability. The Sydney-based firm, according to its website, oversees more than $800 million across its funds. The ABC understand Keyview has no redemption restrictions in place across any of its funds and has no current plans to limit investor liquidity. La Trobe Financial's total exposure to the Bathla Group is approximately $38.1 million. "It comprises four residential loans and one development loan," the firm said in a statement. The development project is approximately 95 per cent complete. The private credit firm added: "We hold the full costs to complete it, and presales cover 89 per cent of the current loan balance. "We expect to recover the loan in full." Trilogy Funds said that, as of yesterday, its exposure to Bathla Group was $29.79 million, relating to two of 131 current loans. "Trilogy Monthly Income Trust continues to operate in the normal course and there are currently no plans to limit investor redemptions," the private lender said in answer to the ABC News questions about the potential for investor redemptions. "Redemption procedures remain unchanged and investors continue to have access to their funds in accordance with normal processes." Concerns more credit provide will limit redemptions Credit funds not exposed to Bathla have told the ABC they are concerned more private credit providers will limit redemptions to avoid investors pulling money out now in fear of not being able to later on. Earlier this week MA Financial announced a temporary redemption limit of up to 1 per cent of its funds under management per month. Bathla Group seeks $20m to keep building Bathla Group's collapse leaves buyers and builders waiting for answers. MA Financial's joint chief executive Chris Wyke told Nine newspapers the action was a "proactive measure in response to the potential for increased redemption activity".

events.title: Nvidia pauses revenue sharing deals with AI cloud companies: Report
events.summary: The chip giant stepped back from the programme last week, adding that it could still revamp the initiative later or fold it into another programme. Nvidia has paused some deals that were part of its new financing initiative that offered credit support to AI cloud companies in exchange for a share of revenue, the Wall Street Journal reported on Aug 27, citing people familiar with the matter. The chip giant stepped back from the programme last week, the Journal said, adding that it could still revamp the initiative later or fold it into another programme. “The new business model... that opens up compute access to the fast-growing AI ecosystem is still in place and continues to evolve due to high demand,” an Nvidia spokesperson said. The reported move comes less than two months after Nvidia announced the programme, designed to support financing needs at small artificial intelligence cloud firms. Nvidia had sought to rent compute capacity back from cloud customers if they were unable to sell it, providing them with a guaranteed buyer and making it easier for the firms to borrow the capital needed to fund their purchases of Nvidia’s AI chips. Under the model, Nvidia would earn revenue on the sale of the hardware itself and then a share of its customers’ cloud revenues derived from Nvidia-powered capacity. Nvidia said in its earnings call this week that the model had the potential to drive billions in revenue over the medium to long term. But investor scrutiny has mounted in recent months as Nvidia pumps money back into the AI ecosystem, stoking fears over its role in so-called circular deals that could artificially inflate demand. The company in August helped arrange US$500 billion (S$635.28 billion) in financing from major US financial institutions for its customers, and also agreed to guarantee up to US$105 billion to help OpenAI lease a massive data centre. The Journal reported that some Nvidia employees expressed concerns to current and potential customers that the initiative could draw antitrust scrutiny, and said there are sensitivities around the extent to which Nvidia can dictate how its customers do business. In the early weeks of the programme, Nvidia irked some potential partners with the extent of control it sought, the report said. Nvidia told some cloud providers they could rent its chips out only to approved customers and signalled that it preferred the capacity be distributed among multiple smaller firms rather than one large customer, the report added. Under the proposed deals, Nvidia would receive 50 per cent of any revenue cloud providers earned through its chips beyond a certain threshold, the Journal said. REUTERS

events.title: Anthropic in talks with chip start up MatX to speed up chip design: Sources
events.summary: The merger talks underscore the AI lab’s ambition to secure the resources and talent needed to build its own chips. Anthropic planned to buy AI chip startup MatX for about US$7 billion but abandoned the deal, shifting focus to a partnership to develop custom chips. Anthropic aims to accelerate in-house chip design to reduce reliance on Nvidia and support its AI models, preparing for a 2026 IPO targeting a US$2 trillion valuation. The company is hiring chip experts and exploring multiple chip designs, balancing purchases from Nvidia, Google, and cloud providers while seeking performance and cost advantages. SAN FRANCISCO – Anthropic discussed buying artificial intelligence chip start-up MatX for roughly US$7 billion (S$8.9 billion), seeking to accelerate efforts to develop custom hardware for its fast-growing AI business, two people briefed on the matter told Reuters. The merger talks, which a third person said have evolved into a discussion about a partnership, underscore the artificial intelligence lab’s ambition to secure the resources and talent needed to build its own chips. The goal is to help Anthropic accelerate its in-house chip development. Reuters is reporting on the discussions for the first time, but could not learn why the talks are no longer active. MatX, founded by former Google tensor processing unit (TPU) engineers, is now seeking to raise new capital at a valuation of about US$4 billion, one of the people said, requesting anonymity to discuss private matters. Anthropic declined to comment on deal talks with MatX. MatX did not respond to a request for comment. As Anthropic scales its Claude family of AI models, the company is looking to produce hardware that can fulfil its voracious appetite for data crunching and reduce its reliance on chips produced by Nvidia. Anthropic, which is expected to list in 2026 , has hired engineering and executive talent to accelerate the chip design process, which could take years. Anthropic’s initial public offering, expected months after SpaceX went public with a US$1 trillion valuation, will chase a valuation of US$2 trillion, which hinges on a 2028 revenue figure of as much as US$200 billion, Reuters reported earlier in August. Anthropic said it is expanding an in-house silicon team to design custom chips that will allow Claude models to run faster and more efficiently. It also plans to keep a multi-chip approach by working with providers from Nvidia to Google. Designing chips is expensive and time-consuming. It can take a year or more to produce a viable piece of hardware, and design costs for a single generation run in the hundreds of millions of dollars. An acquisition of an AI chip start-up such as MatX would give Anthropic in-house design expertise and could help lower costs over the longer term, the people said. MatX has been working on a chip that would be useful for building large AI models in a process called training. Anthropic plans to spend tens of billions of dollars to rent computing power from cloud providers and also plans to buy chips directly. It plans to buy US$36 billion worth of Google’s AI chips, and signed a US$45 billion deal to rent AI cloud computing power from Nscale. It agreed to pay SpaceX US$1.25 billion per month through May 2029 for computing capacity across its data centre clusters. Discussions with other AI chip start-ups The discussions with MatX also suggest Anthropic may be interested in producing a training chip, while other chip start-ups and rival OpenAI pursue processors better suited to generating responses from chatbots, a process known as inference. Anthropic could elect to produce an inference chip as well, the sources said. In recent weeks, Anthropic held meetings with a range of AI chip start-ups. It has not yet elected to make an acquisition. The meetings are an attempt by Anthropic’s engineers and executives to understand the current range of chip design approaches. This week, Anthropic hired Google chip veteran Amir Salek as part of the company’s push into hardware. In June, the AI lab hired former OpenAI chip engineer Clive Chan, who worked on the OpenAI chip unveiled earlier in 2026. The leading AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI have become increasingly focused on custom chips, which can be tailored to their models and workloads. Through this, they hope to create significant performance and economic advantages. At a conference this week, OpenAI boasted that its first custom chip called Jalapeno outperformed a similar processor made by Nvidia. OpenAI executives noted that the chip was more energy efficient in performing inference calculations. Making a custom chip may also help Anthropic hedge against the tight supply of Nvidia’s processors, which Nvidia said in a conference call on Aug 26 would be in short supply through 2027. Google has developed TPUs, while Amazon has built its Trainium and Inferentia chips.

events.title: Scoop: National Democrats and Republicans squeeze local TV stations in ad rate war
events.summary: National Democrats and Republicans are pressuring local TV stations to respond in opposite ways to a new federal court ruling on political ad rates, Axios has learned. Why it matters: How they respond will have a major impact on the fight for control of Congress by deciding which party's ad money goes further in the final stretch of the 2026 midterms . The 4th Circuit Court of Appeals this week overturned an FCC rule extending discounted ad rates for individual congressional campaigns to political parties and super PACs. In other words: The court ruled that outside groups still have to fork over multiple times what the actual candidates pay to run political ads. Democrats tend to do their strongest fundraising at the candidate level while Republicans generally dominate national party and super PAC spending, meaning the decision was a win for Democrats. Driving the news: A pair of Democratic media buyers warned TV stations in a letter first obtained by Axios that they could face legal consequences if they offer discounted rates to outside groups. Doing so "may raise campaign finance concerns," wrote Miles King of Amplify Media and Bradley Perseke of GMMB, because it "risks making an unlawful, unreported corporate in-kind contribution." "Please confirm at your earliest convenience the rates your station intends to offer political party committees and joint fundraising committees for the remainder of the election cycle," they continued. Amplify Media and GMMB work with a slew of Democratic campaigns and groups including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — the House and Senate Democratic campaign arms. Between the lines: Democrats are looking at the federal court ruling as a much-needed win after the Supreme Court ruling last month overturned limits on what political parties could spend in coordination with campaigns. That decision, like the FCC ad rate rule, benefited Republicans' top-heavy fundraising structure in which the national party plays an outsized role. Julie Merz and Devan Barber, the executive directors of the DCCC and DSCC, respectively, said in a statement their groups "dealt Republicans a major blow in their latest attempt to rig the rules in their favor." They added, "Democratic candidates' strong grassroots fundraising amplifying the voice of everyday Americans remains a fundamental advantage in the midterms, and our stronger candidates and better campaigns will secure us House and Senate majorities in November." The other side: Ryan Dollar and Blake Murphy, the top lawyers for the National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, wrote to TV stations that the Democratic letter "should be disregarded." In a letter first obtained by Axios, the two attorneys argued that neither the 4th Circuit Ruling nor Federal Election Commission guidance prohibit stations from offering the discounted rate to outside groups voluntarily. "Broadcasters have long exercised discretion regarding advertising rates in circumstances where an advertiser was not necessarily entitled to a particular statutory benefit," they wrote. What to watch: Dollar and Murphy made their own legal threats, arguing that under Democrats' interpretation of the ruling TV stations have "likely committed years of campaign finance violations" whenever they offered discounted rate to outside groups. "Should your station choose to ... adopt Democrats' campaign finance logic, we intend to file FEC complaints against your station for all advertising you have previously offered," they wrote. Republicans also intend to appeal the 4th Circuit ruling to the Supreme Court, the attorneys said, adding that they "intend to pursue all available remedies to recoup any financial losses should the [FCC] rule be restored."

events.title: Mizuho files case against Radiant World in Singapore court
events.summary: Mizuho Bank is seeking an injunction against Radiant World Corp. Mizuho Bank has initiated legal action against Radiant World in Singapore’s Supreme Court, according to the court system’s website. It is the first legal action taken by a lender to Radiant World to become public since Bloomberg News reported in July on concerns that the iron ore trader had provided banks with falsified documents to secure financing . Mizuho Bank, a unit of Japanese lender Mizuho Financial Group, is seeking an injunction against Radiant World Corp, the main operating unit of the Radiant World group. That implies the Japanese bank is seeking a court order to prevent some action by Radiant World, though it was not yet clear what it was seeking to block. The hearing, which is due to be heard on the morning of Aug 28, was listed as being an originating action and summons related to corporate insolvency. A spokesperson for Mizuho declined to comment. A spokesperson for Radiant World did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The company has previously denied wrongdoing and said that it conducts its business to the highest commercial and legal standards. Filings show that Mizuho is a creditor of Radiant World Corp. events.title: Overcooked? Why robotic pizza makers are failing
events.summary: Robot pizza makers have struggled to make money The "dough feeder". The sauce and cheese modules – even the pepperoni-sprinkler. All lay still. A now defunct duo of robots were supposed to be churning out pizzas at a Moto Pizza restaurant in Seattle. However, in May the pair were rendered "basically useless" when their supplier, Picnic, abruptly shut down. , external Technical support for the robots evaporated at that moment, says Lee Kindell, founder and chief executive of Moto Pizza. He was left wondering what to do with the $160,000 (£118,000), cabinet-like machines and whether buying in pizza bots was really worth it. "I don't know if I want to do a partnership again because of the failures," he says. Lee Kindell's experiment with pizza making machines did not work out The robot pizza-making business has, it's true, been littered with sorry tales of overcooked promises and melting fortunes. Besides Picnic, other companies that have come and gone include Zume , external and Pazzi, which used , external robot arms to assemble pizzas, as well as Basil Street , external , a purveyor of pizza vending machines. Although so-called fast food might seem an easy target for automation, it's proved harder than many expected. Plus, bringing robots into pizza restaurants could take away entry-level jobs in the hospitality sector. Is the future really filled with robotic pizza? "We haven't yet seen any of the success stories materialise the way some people thought they would," admits Sara Senatore, senior restaurants analyst at Bank of America. Her employer has financial interests in multiple high street pizza chains including Papa Johns and Domino's. Food preparation bots are sometimes clumsy – dropping ingredients in the wrong places at times, she explains. Conversely, "Humans are very efficient at making pizza." But Kindell, despite his frustrations with Picnic, is surprisingly undeterred. He is a fan of full automation. "I want to be able to walk up to, let's say, a type of kiosk, put in your order, and it makes a fresh pizza," he tells the BBC. Kindell, who once made all his dough by hand – until an elbow tendon injury forced him to investigate using machines instead, is now working on his own version of a pizza-making robot. He declines to share details but the contraption will make square pan-style pies and that the machine is inspired by the way 3D printers work. If things go well, he says he could have a fully operational version of the device by the summer of 2027. Given that he admits he has "no experience" in robotics, I question why he would want to invest in such a dicey business. Kindell says that failed pizza robot companies have nonetheless generated useful data and made strides in developing their technology. It's just a matter of time before someone gets these things to work, he insists. On jobs, he claims that even "fully autonomous" pizza robots won't threaten workers. Kindell previously used Picnic's robots at T-Mobile Park, home of the Seattle Mariners, a baseball team. Usually, he'd need about 10 people to make pizza in such a setup. With the robots that number fell to just two. But the other eight people were still employed, he says, in roles where they interacted with customers, and advertised the pizza around the stadium. "We had so many more people able to hand out the pizza," says Kindell. "It was so much faster." Appetronix built a robotic pizza maker for the Donatos chain For some pizza robotics engineers, speed is certainly a motivator. Last year at the John Glenn Columbus International Airport in Ohio, Canadian firm Appetronix installed a 24/7 robotic pizza unit for the Donatos pizza chain. Appetronix is working on newer versions of the technology that it claims will assemble pizzas at a furious pace. The goal is to eventually have a pizza sliding out of such machines "every minute", says co-founder and chief executive Nipun Sharma. To that end, his team is investigating methods of depositing sauce onto a pizza base far faster than the 9.5 seconds currently required. "Think of it as a shower head that blasts the sauce in 1.5 seconds," says Sharma. The company is even investigating lasers and ultrasound as potentially speedier methods of slicing pizzas than a traditional knife blade. Many people enjoy hand-crafted pizza, though, I suggest. Doesn't a machine making your dinner take away the human connection we might otherwise feel with food? "What we're going after is a chain market," replies Sharma. "You want the pizza to taste the same every single time." This divide, between businesses focused on repeatability, and those who promise a more artisanal, human-fronted experience, predates robotics. But it will likely shape how and where technology arrives in the world of pizza. Five years ago, Paul Giannone – owner of Paulie Gee's pizza restaurants – vowed to Mashable , external that he would "never" use a robot. "That is still the case," he tells the BBC.

events.title: Military veterans told they owe thousands of pounds over clerical error
events.summary: Royal Navy veteran Andrew Thorburn has been told he owes more than £26,000 Hundreds of former members of the military have had their pensions slashed after receiving letters telling them to repay thousands of pounds because of a clerical error. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed to the BBC that more than 1000 retired service personnel are being pursued for debts. The majority, 335 veterans, were overpaid a total of £5.1m as a result of incorrect National Insurance calculations. The Forces Pension Society said it is aware of a small number of veterans whose debts were wiped after raising a formal complaint. Ray Lawton, 70, was told in July he owed £8,000 following six years of overpayments. Days later, his monthly military pension was cut from £550 to £365. Royal Artillery veteran Ray Lawton has been ordered to repay £8,000 "I haven't got £8,000 to pay out," said Lawton, who served 16 years in the Royal Artillery. "I've got a little bit put aside but nowhere near that much." The Portsmouth-based veteran told the BBC: "I've trusted the army all my life even when I left and I trusted my pension would be right. Then this letter comes and it's just blown it all out." Lawton's letter was sent from a company called Equiniti, which administers the pension scheme on behalf of the MoD. It said an error in its system meant he had been overpaid for years. Lawton is one of many veterans from across the UK who contacted BBC Your Voice after receiving letters out of the blue seeking money they didn't know they owed. The Forces Pension Society, a not-for-profit which supports military retirees, said it is aware of many overpayment cases running into the tens of thousands of pounds. A small number of veterans have been told they owe six-figure sums. The MoD confirmed errors relating to National Insurance adjustments, Pension Sharing Orders (PSO), Early Departure Payments (EDP) and State Pension Age (SPA). It says it is investigating issues on a case-by-case basis. It added that of the 335 veterans affected by National Insurance errors, a third have paid off their debt in full and 52 have an agreed repayment plan in place. So far, of the £5.1m, £304,000 has been paid back. Veterans said they want more clarity about the debt and how it has been calculated. Some have called for it to be wiped. The government said it has a responsibility to recover the funds. An MoD spokesperson told the BBC that it recognises that errors to pension payments "may cause uncertainty", adding that it is contacting veterans and "providing support for anyone who requires it". "Where payments have been made in genuine error, we have a responsibility to recover taxpayer funds and will always seek to do so in a sensitive and proportionate way," the spokesperson added. However, former Conservative defence secretary Penny Mordaunt, said: "While public bodies have a duty to recoup such costs if it makes financial sense to do so, no such assessment has been made in these cases. "There is a compelling case in many instances for the debt to be wiped". Andrew Thorburn says the financial shock has been "absolutely devastating" Lawton does not want the taxpayer to pick up the tab, he is happy to have his pension reduced to the level it should have been but thinks the private company should refund the bill for what he sees as their mistake. "I think they should take responsibility for it because it's not my fault." He served 36 years in the Royal Navy and has been told he owes £26,438. As a result, his pension has been cut by around £650 per month. "I think it's despicable that they are now saying 'yes, we've made this mistake however you're going to pay for it'. How can I forgive the government for that?" He said: "The financial shock is absolutely devastating and it's still ongoing." Barrie Goodwin said the impact of repaying £32,000 would be very difficult RAF veteran Barrie Goodwin contacted Equiniti six years ago after receiving a higher payment than he was expecting. He was told the change was because he had reached state pension age. He's since been notified he was overpaid £32,188 and must hand it back. "I checked, was told it was all correct and now have to repay it," he said. "I'm already cutting back on luxuries. I was helping one of my grandchildren through nursery - that's had to change. "If the debt isn't waived, I will really struggle." Equiniti told the BBC it could not discuss individual cases but recognised the concern caused to pensioners. A spokesperson said it was not responsible for the decision to recoup taxpayers' money but "administration of a scheme of this scale involves multiple organisations, systems and processes over many years". Technology company Sopra Steria has been in charge of the veterans' pension scheme since 2023, and had subcontracted the administration to Equiniti.

events.title: I was spending £700 a month: How I beat my late-night shopping addiction
events.summary: Ella says she would spend her wages "as soon as they hit my account" You may well have been there. It's late, you're scrolling on your phone and suddenly feel a strong urge to buy something - only to wake up the next day and regret it. But what happens when those impulse buys become a habit rather than a one-off? One global study suggests 7% of adults , external experience shopping addiction , external - an uncontrollable urge to spend despite the financial consequences - and younger women are more susceptible. Ella Hewitt, from Liverpool, says her shopping addiction got so bad in 2021 that she was spending up to £700 a month on fast fashion she couldn't afford and sometimes never even wore. "I didn't grow up with much money, so when I got a job I would spend my wages as soon as they hit my account," says the 24-year-old. "That dopamine hit kept me shopping and in the world of social media there is just so much encouragement to do that." She says she would often make purchases on TikTok or Instagram when she was "tired" or "bored", lured by the latest trends on her feeds. Ella says she was "horrified" by the amount she was buying She was working as an HR assistant in a school at the time and her spending meant she couldn't afford to move out of her family home. "Horrified" by how much she was buying, she began using diversionary tactics to control her spending. One was to put anything she felt like buying on a wish list and wait 30 days. "If I still wanted it, I would buy it, but more often than not I'd find the urge had gone," she says. Ella gave herself an imaginary budget of £1,000 each day to spend on imaginary purchases, which "scratched the itch" of shopping without the cost. And she vowed only to buy something if she could afford to "buy it three times". "Overall, I cut my spending by about 60%," says Ella, who now works as an ethical fashion influencer and plans to launch her own clothing brand. "I'm not perfect. There are times when I will buy things because I want it. But I am way more in control." Some people have deleted shopping apps from their phone to make it harder to spend The Ukat Group, which runs addiction treatment centres across the country, says it has seen more people with a shopping addiction and 90% are women. It says there are various signs you may have a , external problem , external , such as your mood improving immediately after making a purchase, or feeling guilty or ashamed afterwards. You may also lie to loved ones about your spending habit or have a home "full of items you don't need or use". Tips to get your spending under control Wait 48 hours or longer before you purchase something. Often the urge will go Delete saved credit card numbers and shopping apps Write a shopping list before you enter a store or visit a site, and stick to it Set a small budget for guilt-free treats, or create an imaginary one Unsubscribe from retailer newsletters and alerts and unfollow influencers Use up products before buying new ones; accessorise rather than buying brand new outfits. Know your triggers: If you shop when you feel lonely, bored or stressed, try exercise or talking with a friend instead Seek help: Citizens Advice, Stepchange, Christians Against Poverty and National Debtline can all offer advice on money problems. Sources: The United Nations Federal Credit Union, Christians Against Poverty 'I would buy anything that was trending' Dish Patel says her spending meant she was "always broke" Dish Patel, 23, from London, says she was spending so much on clothes, food, make-up and skincare as a student that she "maxed out" her £2,500 overdraft and was "always broke". Like Ella, she thinks she was making up for not having much money as a child, but the joy was always short-lived. "The feeling you get when you open your new parcels is always amazing until the dopamine hit dies down and the cycle repeats." Dish, who now works as a financial planner, says she would buy "pretty much anything that was trending" but her biggest vice was scrolling on shopping apps to pass the time. 'I didn't want to spend the money twice' Then, she deleted shopping apps like Asos and Pretty Little Thing from her phone and removed ApplePay to make it harder to buy things in a single click. She even started leaving her bank cards at home when she went to work. "I would bring a packed lunch in and I would buy my train ticket on Trainline the night before... This basically put me in a habit of not spending a single thing and pre-planning my day to ensure I don't spend anything." She also vowed that any time she wanted to buy something, she had to put the same amount of money into her savings or investments. "It worked because I didn't want to spend the money twice." Research last year from Vanquis, a challenger bank, found Gen Z shoppers make more impulse purchases than any other age group , external , closely followed by millennials.

Futu, which reported last week, posted revenue of HK$7.2 billion (US$918 million), up 35.6 per cent, and net income attributable to the shareholders of HK$3.64 billion, up 41.6 per cent. Funded accounts expanded 33.6 per cent to 3.84 million, led for a third straight quarter by Malaysia, with Hong Kong and Singapore also among the top contributors.

events.title: Scoop: Democrats plan bill to counter Trump order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America"
events.summary: House Democrats are planning legislation to counteract the executive order President Trump signed Thursday redesignating Lake Ontario as "Lake America," Axios has learned. Why it matters: Democrats are scrambling to contain the fallout from an escalating economic conflict between the Trump administration and the Canadian government. The collapse of trade talks between the two countries last week triggered 50% tariffs on a slew of Canadian goods, to which Canada has vowed to respond in kind. Driving the news: Democratic Rep. Tim Kennedy, an upstate New Yorker who co-chairs the bipartisan Northern Border Caucus, told Axios in a text message that he is "working on a bill" to respond to Trump's order. Kennedy is one of numerous Democrats who have denounced the renaming, saying in a statement it is evidence that Trump is a "petty, vindictive, failed president." Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), the chair of House Democrats' messaging arm, also slammed the order, saying in a radio interview on Thursday: "I think it's absolutely insane, and I deeply resent it." Catch up quick: The executive order Trump signed directs the Interior Department to update the Geographic Names Information System within 30 days to reflect the name change. "In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation's economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America," the order said. Trump has previously ordered the federal government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America," though it remains unclear if he has the power to rename a body of water shared by multiple countries. Canadian officials have said they will not honor the name change. Reality check: With Republicans in control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats will likely have trouble securing a chance to vote on their legislation.

events.title: Trump’s trade war hands Democrats a campaign-trail gift
events.summary: The News FARMINGTON HILLS, Mich. — President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada is handing a political gift to Democrats in this pivotal battleground state. Democratic candidates across Michigan are unifying against Trump’s 50% tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, hitching Republicans to a trade battle against a trusted neighbor that polls show is unpopular. The alignment is a helpful way for Democrats to change the subject from US-Israel policy, a topic that has bitterly split them in this state in particular. Taking on Trump over Canada trade also helps Democrats sidestep their own past divisions on the issue. The party has long cleaved between pro-business factions and labor allies, and some Democrats — especially in Michigan — remain open to targeted tariffs, not to mention critical of free trade pacts. But at the moment, in a swing state that counts Canada as its top export destination, Democrats are focused on where they agree. “These tariffs are simply about [Trump’s] ego, and he wants us to have to pay for them. And Mike Rogers is going to do nothing but rubber-stamp it,” Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, told supporters Wednesday at a packed banquet hall in the Detroit suburbs. El-Sayed spent both of his appearances in southeast Michigan decrying Rogers, his Republican opponent, as tacitly supportive of Trump’s hefty new tariffs. The levies have so far hit Canadian steel and could affect autos by January. His opposition to Trump’s approach doesn’t extend to all tariffs, however. In an interview with Semafor after his campaign stops, El-Sayed likened past free trade agreements with Canada and Mexico, like NAFTA and USMCA, to “cancers on the American economy. I oppose them outright.” “But the response isn’t just tariffs willy-nilly because you got mad at the prime minister,” El-Sayed added. “The response is a thoughtful, direct tariff policy, akin to chemotherapy for cancer.” He suggested a targeted, “goal-oriented” use of tariffs to protect certain “high growth potential industries,” rolling them back when certain trade benchmarks were met. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Know More The new tariffs’ impact on the cross-border supply chain threatens an auto industry that’s essential to the Michigan economy. Michigan exported $21.2 billion in goods to Canada last year, according to the US trade representative’s office; it’s among the US states most reliant on Canadian trade. Industry representatives in the state are openly warning of electoral consequences for Republican candidates from Trump’s tariffs in multiple states that do significant business with Canada. “The White House’s strategy makes it a lot more difficult … because you have to kind of explain away what this White House’s strategy is,” said the Detroit Regional Chamber of Commerce’s Sandy Baruah, formerly a George W. Bush administration official. It’s not just El-Sayed making the most of the opportunity to hammer Trump’s trade tactics. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson is linking Republican opponent John James to them at every turn, dubbing the Canada tariffs a “John James tax.” In a battleground manufacturing-heavy House district in the Detroit suburbs, Democratic nominee Christina Hines said that “Canada is not the problem.” Hines used her opposition to the tariffs to cast her Republican opponent Mike Bouchard as a loyalist who “falls in line” with Trump. “He’s a really nice young man, but he supports everything that this president does,” she said. “What we need is someone that’s actually going to stand up and fight for us.” Bouchard, in a statement, framed the tariffs as one chapter in negotiations. “For too long, adversarial nations like China have been taking advantage of Canada and America,” Bouchard said. “The President is a great negotiator and is defending American manufacturing. I am hopeful we can resolve this quickly, reach a deal beneficial to both countries, and have fair trade between us. They are an important trading partner and ally.” The View From Canada Across the border, Canadians are digging in for long-term pain at the hands of their onetime ally. Canada has responded with its own retaliatory tariffs and pledged an aid package for affected companies, with Prime Minister Mark Carney commanding public support for the economic pain that will result from pushing back. “We’ve had the sand kicked in our face for the last two years, and we reached a point, because Canadians are notorious for being civil and tolerant — that it’s a breaking point now,” Mike Bradley, the mayor of Sarnia, Ontario, told Semafor in an interview in his office just across the Blue Water Bridge from Port Huron, Mich. “If you think about it,” he added, “most of the economic consequences are going to be on both sides of the border.” Sarnia, a petrochemical center, was already feeling the sting of Trump’s past trade clashes with Canada before the most recent escalation. Bradley called Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario “not that funny” anymore, adding a note of pessimism about the future even after a new president takes office. The US-Canada bond is “like a relationship that goes sideways, and sometimes you can get it back on track, but it’s never usually the same as it was before,” he said. “And sometimes you get divorced.” The View From Republicans Michigan Republicans have largely kept their heads down amid the trade war. Many in the party are generally opposed to tariffs, though some have joined Bouchard in portraying the Canada levies as a negotiating tactic. Rogers and other Republicans have focused instead on Democrats’ associations with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. El-Sayed put distance between himself and Piker on Wednesday following intraparty condemnation of Piker’s comments on American Jews. Nicholas’s view Democrats everywhere, and especially in Michigan, rightly see Trump’s Canada tariffs as a useful unforced error this close to the election. But their agreement on trade isn’t guaranteed to hold should they take power in the Capitol, or reclaim the White House in 2028. Powerful allied groups like the UAW support other tariffs that are aimed at bringing manufacturing jobs back to the US, presaging tough choices ahead for the party. Former President Joe Biden kept many of Trump’s first-term tariffs in place , after all. Bradley, the Canadian mayor, also noticed the conundrum facing the American opposition. “The Democrats should be hitting home runs every day, but the split in the party — you don’t know which Democratic Party is going to be winning in November,” he said. He added a caveat on the new tariffs: “I haven’t seen one Republican of the courage to stand up, at any level elected, to say ‘We do not support this.’” Notable Some of the most profitable cars made by Detroit’s automakers could be hit by the tariffs, The Wall Street Journal reported . events.title: Nasdaq, S&P 500 lifted by Nvidia's forecast; investors eye speech by Fed's Warsh
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City, on Aug 24. Nvidia's strong revenue forecast boosted Nasdaq and technology stocks, highlighting ongoing AI-driven growth despite rising costs and potential memory shortages. S&P 500 and Dow Jones also rose, led by tech gains, while other sectors struggled amid interest rate concerns and geopolitical tensions. Investors now focus on Federal Reserve chair Warsh's upcoming speech for clues on inflation and monetary policy amid mixed economic signals. NEW YORK The technology-heavy Nasdaq outperformed peers at the close of trade on Aug 27, after chip maker Nvidia’s bumper revenue forecast reaffirmed the strength of the AI boom and fuelled gains in technology stocks. Nvidia shares jumped 8.7 per cent after the chip company’s robust forecast met lofty investor expectations, bolstering the view that the tech rally still has room to run as companies at the heart of AI buildout continue to deliver impressive growth. “Nvidia’s results show that the AI boom is not running out of demand... while delivering that growth is becoming more expensive and capital-intensive,” said Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro. Morgan Stanley said in a note on Aug 27 that Nvidia’s forecast for revenue growth of 70 per cent in 2027 is well above Morgan Stanley’s estimate for a 52 per cent rise and that the consensus estimate is closer to 40 per cent. “We would expect Nvidia to continue to knock down barriers to higher growth,” said analyst Joseph Moore in the note. Nvidia has warned that shortages of memory components could curb the pace of the industry’s growth. The S&P 500 closed 55.29 points, or 0.72 per cent, higher at 7,730.99 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 411.16 points, or 1.57 per cent, to 26,541.35. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 105.56 points, or 0.2 per cent, to 53,569.44. US chip-linked stocks broadly rose, with the semiconductor index notching a 2.3 per cent gain. The S&P 500 Information Technology sector rose 3.4 per cent, making it the best gainer among the S&P 500’s 11 constituents, which were mostly in the red. “While Nvidia’s earnings beat and strong guidance restarted the party, it’s apparent that not all sectors of the market were invited,” said Charlie Ripley, senior investment strategist at Allianz Investment Management. “Market headwinds continue to be a factor as higher interest rates, geopolitical tensions and global trade, among other things, are playing a role in the weakness seen across other sectors.” Brent crude prices jumped by more than US$2 per barrel on Aug 27, after a Wall Street Journal report that said US President Donald Trump is not interested in returning to terms of a memorandum of understanding reached with Iran in June. Salesforce surged 22.6 per cent after raising annual revenue and profit forecasts, and rolling out a new plug-in integrated with Anthropic’s Claude AI models. CrowdStrike climbed 20.5 per cent after the cybersecurity software provider raised its annual revenue forecast and topped second-quarter earnings estimates. The Salesforce and CrowdStrike reports calmed worries that advanced AI tools could upend the traditional software industry, boosting investor appetite for beaten-down software stocks and narrowing the gap with semiconductors, which are seen as the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom. With Nvidia results out, investor attention turns to Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh’s first Jackson Hole address on Aug 28 for hints on the central bank’s stance on the latest inflation data and the US Treasury’s efforts to tame yields. “A common theme from Warsh has been his focus on the supply side of the economy and we expect that to remain the focus,” said Christopher Hodge, chief US economist for Natixis. “I highly doubt that Warsh will be too declarative in his assessments of what’s to come, but it would not be surprising if he expressed some scepticism about previous policy assumptions and generally struck an anti-doctrinaire approach.” A hotter-than-expected Personal Consumption Expenditures reading on Aug 26 muddied the policy outlook, dampening some of the optimism generated by a benign consumer inflation report earlier this month. Two Fed officials shared their ongoing concerns about the inflation outlook on Aug 27, reiterating their stance on rate hikes to combat price pressures. Meanwhile, the number of Americans seeking unemployment benefits for the first time fell for a second week, while the overall number slid to the lowest in a month, signalling a stable labour market. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 1.02-to-1 ratio on the New York Stock Exchange. There were 192 new highs and 82 new lows on the NYSE. On the Nasdaq, 2,570 stocks rose and 2,325 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 1.11-to-1 ratio. The S&P 500 posted 15 new 52-week highs and 8 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 73 new highs and 85 new lows.

events.summary: Taiwan’s legislature approved a plan to spend more than $7 billion on drones over the next six years, part of the island’s push to deter a potential attack from China. Taiwan’s drone manufacturing has largely been scaled for export, but the new budget — although watered down — could boost domestic demand for drones and strengthen local supply chains, allowing the sector to mass produce drones even under bombardment. Taiwan’s vice president noted the island was inspired by how Ukraine had built up its drone capabilities from the “ battlefield of blood and tears. ” — Brendan Ruberry

( Team Global Express ) Team Global Express has reversed its decision to stop delivering to parts of regional Tasmania. Residents had told the ABC they were forced to spend hours on the road to collect their deliveries from the depot, despite paying for a door-to-door service. The company's executive chair, Christine Holgate, visited Miena in central Tasmania to speak with an affected resident and tell him the deliveries would restart. A delivery company has reinstated services to regional Tasmania, after residents raised complaints with the ABC. In recent months, Team Global Express stopped delivering online orders to Miena, Liawenee, Waddamana, Levendale, Tunnack, Bradys Lake, Bronte Park, Derwent Bridge, Lake St Clair, Maydena and Colebrook. Despite paying for deliveries to be sent to their homes, residents received text messages saying they had seven days to pick up their packages from the company's depot at Hobart Airport . The company cited operational challenges for its drivers as the reason for the decision, including unsafe road conditions in winter. On Thursday, the executive chair of Team Global Express, Christine Holgate, flew to Tasmania to visit Miena resident Michael Walls, who had told the ABC he was not willing to make a four-hour round trip to collect his packages when he had paid for delivery. For Michael Walls, the round trip to pick up his packages from the Hobart depot would have taken four hours. ( ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough ) Mr Walls said the visit was a success. "Ms Holgate confirmed that Team Global Express has reversed their decision to stop delivering to large parts of central Tasmania," he told ABC Northern Tasmania. "Team Global Express will now resume [delivering] to all areas they previously cancelled. "Ms Holgate also said she would like to apologise to their customers for this decision and said it was their local Tasmanian management decision to cancel the service and that it was not known by their national office. Christine Holgate visited Miena on Thursday to speak with an affected resident. ( ABC News: Marcus Stimson ) A spokesperson for the company confirmed the reversal. "Christine is very grateful to Michael for raising the matter," they said. The Tasmanian government welcomed the decision, saying it was an example of what could be achieved when regional communities made their voices heard and businesses were prepared to listen. "This is a very welcome outcome for people living and doing business in rural and regional Tasmania," Consumer Affairs Minister Guy Barnett said. "Reliable freight and parcel delivery services are crucial in rural communities, where residents and small businesses may otherwise face hours of travel simply to collect an item they have paid to have delivered. "I thank Team Global Express executive chair Christine Holgate for taking the time to come to Tasmania, listening to the concerns raised on behalf of our regional communities and acting quickly to find a way forward.

events.title: Trump orders new name for Lake Ontario in provocative trade war twist
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Trump orders renaming of Lake Ontario amid US-Canada trade war Donald Trump's order instructs the name change to be reflected in government maps, contracts and other documents. ( Reuters: Evan Vucci ) Donald Trump has signed an order demanding Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America. Mr Trump is determined to punish Canada after its leaders rejected a trade deal and imposed reciprocal tariffs of up to 50 per cent on US imports. Canada maintains its own database of place names and will not recognise Mr Trump's order. Donald Trump has changed the name of a lake on the US-Canada border in a provocative twist in the trade war between the neighbouring nations. The US president signed an order demanding Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America, following through on repeated threats made via troll posts on social media in recent days. "Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade, very sadly," Mr Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, where he sat beside revised maps on large poster boards, including one headlined "Making the Great Lakes Even Greater". Mr Trump is determined to punish Canada after its leaders last week rejected a trade deal they said was too one-sided . Mr Trump initially responded by announcing tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Canadian imports. Canada retaliated with reciprocal tariffs on US products . Analysts say the escalating trade war will be damaging for both countries. The trade war between the US and Canada escalates again as Canadian leaders outline a major retaliation against Donald Trump's latest wave of tariffs. Mr Trump's order means the lake's name must be changed within 30 days in the Geographic Names Information System, the official database of US place names. It also requires government maps, contracts and other documents be edited to reflect the new name. Canada maintains its own place-names database and will not recognise the US order. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the name came from an Indigenous word meaning: "The lake is beautiful, the lake is big." The name predates both the Canadian Confederation and the formation of the US, Mr Carney wrote on X. "We know that America is changing," Mr Carney said. "Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms. Lake Ontario is one of the five Great Lakes of North America, the others being Lake Superior, Lake Michigan, Lake Huron and Lake Erie. It straddles the border between the Canadian province of Ontario and the state of New York, whose Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, responded to Mr Trump's order by saying: "We won't be calling it that." The name change is reminiscent of Mr Trump's order to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America shortly after his return to the presidency last year, on the grounds "we do most of the work there". That name change was also recorded in the US's official place names database. But the body of water, to the US's south-east and Mexico's north-east, is still internationally recognised as the Gulf of Mexico.
